articles.title: France announces curfews as government grapples with unrest
articles.description: France announced partial curfews in Paris and other cities on Monday after weekend demonstrations over soaring prices degenerated into some of the worst street violence in recent years. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu did not rule out imposing a state of emergency after the interior minister said police had “lost control”. Tourists in Paris had a taste of the disruption on Monday when they found the Louvre closed because of a small group of student protesters. Facing accusations that it failed to anticipate and respond to the violence, the government has vowed to re-establish order, while officials scrambled to contain public anger. The unrest , erupting just six months before France elects a successor to President Emmanuel Macron, threatened to continue, with organisers calling for a new round of protests next Saturday. Authorities said partial curfews would be enforced from Monday evening to Tuesday morning in a number of cities including Paris, Lille and Lyon, to protect businesses. In the capital, a curfew was ordered from 11pm (2am PKT), while demonstrations were banned from 8pm. “I’m absolutely determined to restore public order”, Lecornu said. Other European countries have also seen demonstrations over rising prices, with smaller clashes breaking out in Milan and Belgium over the weekend and protests simmering in Spain and Portugal. Some half a million people turned out across France on Saturday to denounce the surging cost of living, a culmination of four weeks of protests that began with students demanding better conditions at high schools. What started as peaceful demonstrations descended into violence in many cities, as masked groups attacked law enforcement, broke into public buildings and set some ablaze, looted shops, and set fire to cars, bicycles and scooters. Listings for ‘stolen goods’ On Monday, France’s digital minister, Anne Le Henanff, urged online resale platforms to remove listings for “stolen items” following Saturday’s looting and summoned representatives of companies including Vinted and eBay. CCTV footage shows a masked group breaking into a jewellery shop in Lyon, France, October 17, 2026, in this screengrab obtained from a handout video. — Reuters After the weekend scenes of chaos, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez offered his resignation, but Macron refused to accept it. More than 2,500 people were arrested and nearly 1,000 members of the security forces injured. Protesters were also hurt, with one demonstrator’s hand blown off by a police crowd-control grenade. Macron acknowledged failures in the government response, which had seen 60,000 law enforcement personnel deployed on Saturday. Nationwide, more than 2,513 people have been taken into police custody since the weekend, Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said. He added that 67 had been jailed and “dozens” of criminal cases opened. Darmanin also said authorities would use facial recognition on social media to identify perpetrators. At least 3,000 shops were damaged, with the cost running into hundreds of millions of euros. In an address to the nation on Sunday, Macron slammed the “unbridled” violence. The European Union called the violence “unacceptable” but warned that the right to peaceful protest “must be protected” in France. Germany condemned the violence and updated its travel advice for France, saying “further outbreaks of violence in the coming days cannot be ruled out”. China has warned citizens travelling to France to be aware of risks and take safety precautions, state broadcaster CCTV reported. Louvre blocked In Paris on Monday, a dozen demonstrators blocked the entrance to the Louvre, the most visited museum in the world, while bewildered tourists looked on. “We don’t want to get involved. We want to stand back and get away from them,” Pat Boland, a tourist from Australia, said of the protests. The pensioner, 73, spoke to AFP outside barricades that had been erected at the Louvre, which was closed because a small group of protesters stood by its famed glass pyramid entrance. Protesters and students from art and culture schools block the entrance to the Louvre Museum during a demonstration in support of a high school student movement demanding better school conditions and government action, in Paris, France, October 19, 2026. — Reuters The unrest has flared before presidential elections in April and May that will elect a new French president after a decade of centrist Macron. Marine Le Pen, the far-right presidential candidate , is riding high in the polls. The government has accused ultra-left groups of stoking the violence to boost the chances of the far-left firebrand Jean-Luc Melenchon in the presidential polls. The interior minister and intelligence services were to meet late Monday to discuss the violence. Europe During the weekend, clashes broke out on the sidelines of a cost-of-living demonstration in Milan. “I’m very worried because it’s a new phenomenon, which also originates from an international scenario and therefore feeds itself,” mayor Giuseppe Sala said. In Belgium, police fired tear gas and water cannon to disperse protesters in Brussels and Liege. In Spain protesters have set up tents in the heart of Madrid to denounce soaring housing costs, with similar encampments going up in neighbouring Portugal’s main cities of Lisbon and Porto.

These decisions will be made on the ground, by the prefects, in coordination with the mayors,” he said. Police confirmed the night had passed without major incidents across France. Several cities, including Paris, the southwestern city of Bordeaux and Nice on the French Riviera, introduced partial curfews on Monday in response to urban unrest that followed weeks of student demonstrations over poor learning conditions in high schools. This photograph shows a fire burning and destroying the city hall after a group of individuals forced entry into the building during ongoing protest action against the “high cost of living”, in Limoges, central France on Oct 17, 2026. — AFP/File While some restrictions, such as those in Paris, initially applied only for the night from Monday to Tuesday, others, particularly in Bordeaux and Nice, were set to remain in force for several days. During the night, a helicopter flew over the French capital’s Place de la Republique, one of the epicentres of the unrest, sweeping a powerful searchlight across the square to monitor compliance with the curfew. In Lyon, despite a ban on demonstrations, around 500 people gathered on Monday evening outside the tourism office that was set on fire, to show support for shopkeepers affected by looting, according to organisers. The word “LYON” had been spelled out on the ground with candles. People lit candles in front of the Lyon tourist office before a partial curfew in Lyon on October 19, 2026, following weekend demonstrations over soaring prices degenerated into some of the worst street violence in recent years. —AFP A banner hung on a fence nearby read “Anti-Rioters Lyon” and “Doucet Resign”, referring to Green mayor Gregory Doucet, an AFP journalist said. Under pressure, the government scheduled another series of emergency meetings on Tuesday, including talks involving representatives of major social media platforms. Finance Minister Roland Lescure pledged support measures for shopkeepers and craftspeople. articles.title: As France erupts, Europe's far right gains from fuel-price anger ahead of elections
articles.description: The tractors rolling into the town of Gela on the southern tip of Europe are flying the Sicilian flag, emblazoned with Medusa, three bent legs and ears of wheat, a reminder of the island’s role as a breadbasket since Roman times. But the farmers are not bringing in a harvest. They are protesting. As soaring fuel prices squeeze household budgets and businesses across Europe, cost-of-living pressures are driving unrest and giving fresh momentum to far-right parties ahead of elections next year in countries including France, Italy and Poland. Parties once considered fringe had already been gaining ground, with voters from motorists in rural France to young men in Germany’s former Communist east looking for alternatives. The US-Iran war, which erupted in February and sent energy prices sharply higher, has compounded the challenge for governments already struggling to contain inflation, support growth and rein in spending. The discontent has spilled onto the streets. In France, demonstrations that began over deteriorating school facilities in Paris’ northern suburbs have morphed into some of the country’s worst unrest in decades, with shops looted, buildings torched and a 19th-century town hall in Limoges set on fire. “Why am I here? Well, quite simply, I find the current cost of living truly terrifying,” said Quentin Leviloux, a 21-year-old protester in Nantes. “Just think of people who earn barely the minimum wage, when you look at the cost of food, fuel, and everything else. Its terrifying how incredibly expensive things have become.” The European Commission estimates the Iran conflict has cost Europe roughly 100 billion ($112 billion) through disrupted trade and energy markets. Gas prices have jumped about 140 per cent and diesel prices have doubled. In a weekend address, French President Emmanuel Macron acknowledged the “legitimate demands” of protesters angered by rising living and fuel costs, while condemning those responsible for violence and looting. “We must never confuse them with those who destroyed, vandalised and looted,” he said. Protests erupt across Europe Violence has also erupted elsewhere. In the wealthy northern Italian city of Milan, police clashed on Sunday with protesters hurling stones and looting stores during demonstrations over poor public services and rising living costs. In Gela, on Sicily’s southern coast, farmers say fuel costs have made operating machinery prohibitively expensive. “We cultivate the land, we harvest debts,” said one banner. A man throws a plastic traffic cone through a burning barricade amid clashes during a day of demonstrations against the cost of living and rising fuel prices in Paris as part of nationwide protests called by the “Yellow Vests” movement, joined by French high school and university students, Oct 19. —Reuters/File “We are completely at a standstill,” said Arcangelo Gambino, a farmers’ representative in Caltanissetta province. “The (fuel) cost has more than doubled.” Roadblocks by truckers, farmers and steelworkers have disrupted transport across parts of southern Italy, contributing to local fuel shortages and concerns over supermarket supplies. Tens of thousands marched through Lisbon on Saturday over low wages, housing costs and the rising cost of living, increasing pressure on Portugal’s centre-right government. In Spain, the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home sparked nationwide demonstrations over housing shortages and soaring rents, helping trigger a snap election next month. Belgium has also seen demonstrations, while large rallies in Albania have been driven by anger over perceived government corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards. The protests reflect broader economic anxieties that are increasingly shaping politics across the continent. Concerns about purchasing power have become “a major driver of populist politics” across Europe, said Gilles Ivaldi, a political scientist at Sciences Po. Politicians on both the hard right and hard left have increasingly argued that restoring energy ties with Russia would help lower costs, challenging Europe’s mainstream consensus on support for Ukraine. Le pen makes fuel prices a campaign issue The latest energy shock comes after years of economic strain following the pandemic and the fallout from Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine . In France, rising energy costs have provided an explosive backdrop to next April’s presidential election. Macron’s government is struggling with a ballooning budget deficit and pressure from bond markets. Frontrunner Marine Le Pen of the far-right National Rally and hard-left veteran Jean-Luc Melenchon have both made fuel prices central planks in their campaigns. Rising fuel prices are clearly an issue that boosts Marine Le Pen, said Ivaldi. I think this is an issue she has owned for quite some time.” Since the Iran war began, Le Pen’s ratings have improved while Macron’s have slipped, according to polling by Elabe. Le Pen’s proposal to sharply cut value-added tax on fuel has attracted broad public support. Analysts say the issue resonates strongly with her core voters in rural and semi-rural areas where car travel is often essential. Calls to restore Russia ties In neighbouring Germany, the Alternative for Germany (AfD) is leading national opinion polls after strong gains in local elections. The cost of living topped Germans’ concerns for a fifth straight year in a survey published this month. German inflation spiked to nearly a three-year high in September, with energy price inflation rising to 14.9pc, handing ammunition to the AfD to attack Chancellor Friedrich Merz. The AfD is pushing to restore energy ties with Russia, arguing that Berlins support for Ukraine is needlessly self-sabotaging at a time when Europes largest economy and many of its energy-hungry companies are struggling. Past experience indicates a link between high energy prices and voter turnout for the AfD, said Jan Steckel, professor for the political economy of climate change at the Technical University of Munich. A protestor holds a sign reading “Generations 6-7 redoes May 68” in front of a fire at the Boulevard des Capucines during a demonstration to protest against the “high cost of living”, in Paris, France on October 17, 2026. — AFP Populist parties often frame energy costs as avoidable and attribute them to government policy choices … rather than to the underlying geopolitical shocks that drive them,” he said. These geopolitical shocks are … much more difficult to explain. And I think this is why incumbent parties often struggle.” The argument is gaining traction elsewhere. In Italy, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni faces growing competition from National Future, a new far-right party led by former army general Roberto Vannacci that advocates restoring gas links with Russia. In Poland, one of Ukraine’s staunchest supporters, concern over energy bills is helping boost support for the far-right Confederation of the Polish Crown. Its leader, Grzegorz Braun, has called for a return to buying Russian oil and gas, making the case alongside AfD politicians in Lubmin, where the damaged Nord Stream pipelines land in Germany. I love the smell of Russian gas in the morning, he said.

articles.title: France riots become Republican midterm boogeyman
articles.description: As the French right-wing National Rally is seizing on fiery protests in the country for its pre-election pitch, so are President Trump and his Republican allies in the U.S. The big picture: The Trump administration has used the unrest, which began over education grievances , to bolster its messaging on immigration and the threat of "communists," a group Trump has repeatedly claimed is threatening American civilization. Driving the news: "When you see burning steeples and raging fires in France, just remember that is what the radical 'Dumocrats' want to do to America," Trump said before a Kansas rally crowd Monday. He claimed France was being "conquered, looted and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists and communists who hate Christianity" and "the Western civilization itself." Speaking earlier to reporters, the president claimed, without evidence, that the situation in France was about "immigration, not schools." He's repeatedly blamed immigration for the protests. The White House referred Axios to the president's Truth Social post echoing that rhetoric. Catch up quick: Localized demonstrations by high school students that began in Paris last month have broadened into a massive nationwide movement over poor school conditions and cost of living, sparking thousands of arrests and clashes between police and protesters, Axios' Bec Falconer reports. The civil unrest gave way to rioting and looting, leading French President Emmanuel Macron to condemn "unrestrained violence" by "insurrectionist elements from radical far-left groups, joined by numerous criminals," per AP . Some 550,000 people demonstrated in France Saturday, per the Interior Ministry, though Reuters reported that a key union estimated 800,000. On the sidelines, "thugs" chose "violence," per a translation of the Interior Ministry's statement , which added that some 500 police officers and firefighters were injured. The forceful police response to student demonstrators has also been scrutinized , sparking dozens of probes into officer conduct. Zoom out: Some U.S. Republicans have followed Trump in evoking the protests, which have spread to other countries , to rally voters and condemn immigration . Vice President Vance wrote on X , " Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion," sharing a video of a historic town hall reportedly set ablaze by masked protesters, per AFP. "This is the future congressional Democrats seek for your country," Vance contended. Yes, but: Macron, per a translation of his nationwide address over the weekend protests, said the hundreds of thousands of demonstrators had " legitimate demands" and should not be conflated with violent rioters. He said those concerns included the cost of living and fuel price spikes triggered by the war in Iran. The bottom line: The spiraling violence has created a global shock that Trump is harnessing as a boogeyman ahead of an uphill midterm battle. articles.title: State Bank of India reports cyberattack involving nearly 3,900 customer records
Season of uprisings
articles.description: PERHAPS the most unfortunate aspect of the latest French popular uprising is that it may well facilitate Marine Le Pen’s journey to the Élysée Palace. The far-right contender for the presidency poses as the law-and-order saviour for a France that no longer exists, focusing — like the Trump regime — on immigration as the source of every societal woe. The unrest that erupted in September with students from a couple of public high schools complaining about shrinking resources and inadequate facilities ballooned into a much broader rebellion. By last weekend, the protests had extended beyond disenchanted pupils and their parents and teachers to a far wider cross-section of society complaining about the cost of living — alongside the usual panoply of vandals, looters, and arsonists. The latter were on the fringes of largely peaceful demonstrations but inevitably grabbed the headlines, featuring images of shattered shopfronts and the historic Limoges town hall in flames. To be fair, though, almost every report I came across acknowledged the carnivalesque aspect of the huge marches, distinguishing it from the criminality of opportunist gangs. Even President Emmanuel Macron made that distinction in his unimpressive address to the nation on Sunday, but offered little more than retribution for the offenders and a dialogue with ‘stakeholders’. Earlier, in response to the students’ demands, the government promised 3,000 more substitute teachers, but that’s not likely to alleviate concerns. With France’s national debt at 119pc of its GDP, the usual excuse is that the state cannot afford to throw money at education (or health), let alone consider social spending that might ease wider cost-of-living woes. Yet economists have worked out that a relatively small increase in inheritance tax for the wealthiest one per cent of heirs would suffice for a substantial investment in education, while Thomas Piketty notes that the growth in private wealth means “France has never been richer”, notwithstanding its public debt. Echoes of 1968 have been discerned in the events in France. That’s a familiar story. In Europe alone, economic woes have prompted mass protests from the Iberian Peninsula to Albania. The rough end of the European housing crisis featured prominently in Spain, where citizens revolted once more after 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was forcibly evicted from her home of 70 years because she could not afford the 230pc rent increase. She died a fortnight later, prompting more outrage. A snap election has been called for Nov 29 after the right-wing opposition thwarted two decrees from the Pedro Sánchez government aimed at redressing tenants’ woes. Similar concerns have brought Portuguese citizens to the streets, and broader affordability worries have led to protests in Belgium and Italy. In Albania, meanwhile, the ‘flamingo’ protests that grew from environmental concerns over an island that Donald Trump’s daughter and son-in-law sought to colonise have expanded to include less esoteric concerns, spreading from the capital Tirana to various other cities and demanding the departure of the prime minister and opposition leader. La France Insoumise, the only viable left-wing force in French politics, has backed the agitators and condemned the violence, but should LFI leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon make it into the second round of the next presidential election, there’s little doubt that the extreme centre epitomised by Macron will opt for Le Pen, effectively authorising a second Vichy regime. Similar patterns are likely to be witnessed in the rest of the continent. Happily, the prospects in India differ. There is no scope for complacency, but the Cockroach Janta Party and its allies have clearly rattled the Modi regime. Its demise may not be imminent, but it’s no longer inconceivable. Every country deserves a Neha Bora. Several commentators in Pakistan have lamented the lack of parallels. Sorrow and angst were expressed after 34 pupils and a teacher were killed last week in a roof collapse at a private Peshawar school. In many other countries, such a tragedy would have prompted demands for a nationwide reckoning, not least because of the criminally low state spending on education. But Pakistan, it seems, has better things to do. Echoes of 1968 have been discerned in the events in France. Back then, university students, eventually backed by the unionised working class, briefly chased away Charles de Gaulle. He returned in apparent triumph but was gone within a year. Meanwhile, our first field marshal, hailed by his Western sponsors as Pakistan’s de Gaulle, departed for good after a student-led popular rebellion in 1968-69. It isn’t necessary to condone what followed to hail the demise of the Ayub regime as a tremendous achievement. But perhaps it’s also a reminder to be careful what you wish for, given what followed in the next decade. mahir.dawn@gmail.com Published in Dawn, October 21st, 2026

articles.title: ‘How can France stop Marine Le Pen’? Our Europe columnists answered your questions on protests and politics in France
articles.description: Guardian Europe columnists Rokhaya Diallo and Alexander Hurst answered your questions about the recent protests in France, the role of the French police, foreign influence and the upcoming presidential election. Michael Wolfcarius asks: I cannot understand why the Guardian is selecting dots instead of joining them. France may have developed into the big story for many reasons, many of which have yet to be discussed, but it is not the only place where seemingly small incidents grew into massive protests, some also quite violent; Spain, Italy, Serbia and Albania come to mind. The crystallising reason may be different but the conditions leading up to it are quite similar. Can you put all these events into perspective, context and relation? There are obviously underlying currents making it difficult for people to refrain from making themselves ‘heard’. Rokhaya: I agree that these movements deserve to be considered together, while at the same time, recognising their different specific national contexts. Housing in Spain, living costs and public services in Italy and France, and corruption in Serbia and Albania are bringing people onto the streets. These concerns touch the foundations of a decent life and people’s ability to shape their future. What connects them, in my view, is the widening gap between what people need and what political institutions seem willing to deliver. These incidents that have led to protests are not “small .” Serbia’s movement began after a deadly railway-station canopy collapse, which became a focus for anger over corruption and accountability. My reading is that these protests express a crisis of political responsiveness. Alexander: I think people in all these places – Albania, Spain, France – feel that the political systems that exist aren’t capable of dealing with the sheer scale and nature of the crises facing us, and they’re responding to a sense of ‘loss of control’ (the Brexit campaign really did strike upon a brilliant slogan) over where their societies are headed. There is a general social sense that has flipped from “this is broken, but things can and will get better”, which gives people a stake in the institutions around them, to “this is broken and things can and will get worse”. The impact of the arrival of AI has been understated. Not just on labour markets, or on the environment, but ontologically. The investment pitch of the most powerful companies in the world, the ones amassing trillion dollar valuations, isn’t just that X-subset of jobs are replaceable, it’s that human beings themselves are replaceable. That the things we do fundamentally don’t matter, and that their goal is to bring this into being. I think that feeling is there even if we don’t immediately put our finger on it in those terms. articles.title: Macron takes aim at Trump for using France riots for election gain
articles.description: President Emmanuel Macron on Wednesday took an apparent swipe at counterpart Donald Trump of exploiting France’s riots for advantage in the US midterm election battle, as Paris prepared for more protests this weekend. Macron, speaking during a visit to Qatar, implied that Trump, and possibly Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is also in election mode , made “stupid comments” on the unrest for political gain, though he did not name either leader. “There are people who campaign at France’s expense — leaders who are in campaign mode, whether here in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic,” he told reporters in Doha. Macron made his remarks as he and his government struggled to get on top of a crisis that has scarred France’s image both abroad and in financial markets, six months ahead of presidential elections to choose his successor. France’s government has admitted it “lost control” in the frenzy of street violence that erupted last weekend, when masked youths clashed with police, looted shops and vandalised public buildings. Trump has sought to link the “revolution” in France to “migrants, jihadists, and communists” as he campaigned for his Republican party in the United States on his anti-immigration messaging. He also on Tuesday hailed French far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who shares his ideologies, as a conservative voice, with surveys putting her as the frontrunner in France’s presidential race. Trump’s ally Netanyahu, facing his own tough election battle, on Tuesday argued that France had been hit by an “invasion of extremist Islam”. Several analysts have dismissed the claims that migrants were driving France’s protests. Curfews The unrest overshadowed demonstrations held on Saturday in which more than half a million people marched nationwide against the cost of living. Those rallies followed four weeks of student protests that have closed many schools across France. Since the rioting — the worst France has seen in years — and ahead of further cost-of-living demonstrations this coming Saturday, Macron’s government has warned it will brook no further violence. Authorities in Paris and several other cities imposed nighttime curfews Monday and Tuesday in certain zones prone to protests or looting. Macron said that on Thursday he would chair a meeting of key ministers and intelligence officials to receive a “detailed account” of what happened last weekend. French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, who on Wednesday held a meeting with union leaders organising marches, has vowed a “massive” police deployment for the fresh demonstrations called for Saturday by the Yellow Vest movement protesting rising inflation. The convulsion in France, the EU’s second-biggest economy after Germany, has rattled financial markets already nervous about the country’s growing debt pile and deficit. The yield on the French government’s benchmark 10-year bond has been rising, and on Wednesday surpassed five percent as investors demanded a higher return given the fiscal woes. A rising yield signifies a drop in bond prices. The Paris stock market also fell. On Friday, the Moody’s ratings agency is expected to lower its grade on France’s public debt. The country’s political landscape is so fragmented that Lecornu has little chance of winning swift parliamentary consensus for a cost-cutting budget that needs to be adopted before the end of this year. Le Pen leads race The latest survey, carried out by Ifop in the wake of the riots, suggested Le Pen would lead first-round voting intentions by a wide margin and far-left candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon emerged as her most likely opponent in the runoff. France’s neighbours Italy and Belgium have also started to experience similar unrest, on a smaller scale. Italy’s government has ordered 500 troops to Milan to stem street violence there. Macron said that “we don’t need a state of emergency” that would likewise permit soldiers to reinforce police against rioters, adding that “we have the means” already at authorities’ disposal, such as curfews. While the partial curfews have led to a calming of the situation in Paris and elsewhere, they have disrupted travel for commuters looking to take urban rail after 11pm (2am PKT). “It’s quite disconcerting,” said one Paris commuter who gave only his first name, Louis, when he found his line closed. But “if it can prevent further acts of vandalism… then yes, I think it’s a good thing”, he said. The Yellow Vest movement behind last weekend’s demonstrations announced on Wednesday that it had formally told authorities it planned to hold its Paris march on Saturday starting from Bastille square. The movement also wants to hold follow-up nationwide demonstrations on Nov 5. The images broadcast around the world of France’s street violence last weekend have prompted several countries, including the United States, China and Germany, to issue travel advisories for their citizens in France.

articles.title: Governo francês anuncia proibição de protestos considerados ilegítimos
articles.description: O presidente francês, Emmanuel Macron, anunciou nesta quinta-feira (22) a proibição, nos próximos dias, de ações de protesto avaliadas como “ilegítimas”. O anúncio foi feito após reunião com representantes dos serviços de informações e ministros. Para as manifestações organizadas por estruturas como os sindicatos vão ser definidos trajetos alternativos. O objetivo, segundo o governo, é proteger os estabelecimentos comerciais. Notícias relacionadas: Tensões voltam a crescer; França contabiliza custos de protestos. França: estudantes prometem continuar luta após primeira vitória. França quer impor toques de recolher após fim de semana com tumultos. Em breve declaração, à qual dedicou pouco de mais de três minutos, o chefe de Estado francês citou grupos de extrema-esquerda “sediciosos” (indivíduos que incitam atos de rebelião), que as autoridades acreditam estar na base dos desacatos, roubos e furtos ocorridos no último sábado (17) em diferentes cidades do país. Macron classificou os grupos de “ultraesquerda de extrema periculosidade”, acusando-os de pretender “derrubar a República”. “Tivemos, simultaneamente, atos políticos e até sediciosos, conduzidos por grupos organizados de ultraesquerda que visam derrubar a República”, acusou o presidente francês, após reunião, no Palácio do Eliseu, com todos os serviços de informações. A menos de 48 horas de nova mobilização na França, o governo procura atenuar a pressão acentuada pelo cenário de confrontos urbanos de 17 de outubro. “Firmeza” é a palavra mais ouvida nos corredores do poder em Paris. Nos últimos dias, o primeiro-ministro francês, Sébastien Lecornu, apelou aos partidos para que escolham “entre a violência e a República”, isolando nas críticas o partido de extrema-esquerda A França Insubmissa, de Jean-Luc Mélenchon . Lecornu convocou os partidos, prometendo “transparência” sobre as “dificuldades encontradas” na resposta aos acontecimentos de sábado. Diante do balanço sobre roubos, furtos e estragos em cerca de 3 mil lojas, no último fim de semana, os comerciantes temem o que possa acontecer no sábado . “A preocupação é máxima”, resumiu Pierre Bosche, presidente da Confederação dos Comerciantes da França, em declarações à agência France-Presse. "A mão não deve tremer" As autoridades prometem dispositivo policial em larga escala para o próximo sábado, com recurso a veículos blindados e a várias unidades de elite. Nas palavras de Macron, “a mão não deve tremer no topo do Estado”. 'Generational rage': Young Europeans fight to be heard
articles.description: From blockaded schools in Rome to tent camps in Madrid and street protests in France, young people across Europe are turning their anger on a political class they say is not listening. Their demands vary, but they are united in wanting to make their often marginalised voices heard, sometimes even with radical methods in the face of heavy-handed policing. “We are fighting and taking our future in our hands,” said Damiano Fusa, 18, a student at Rome’s Cavour high school, the first to be occupied in a wave of student takeovers that has spread across the Italian capital. “We’re not represented by anyone,” Fusa told AFP, criticising both Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s hard-right coalition and previous centre-left governments for cutting education funding and ignoring young people’s needs. Protesters and students from art and culture schools block the entrance to the Louvre Museum during a demonstration in support of a high school student movement demanding better school conditions and government action, in Paris, France, October 19, 2026. — Reuters Hundreds of thousands of high school and university students have rallied in France, Italy, Spain and other European countries in recent weeks, with some protests descending into violence. Governments have largely focused on restoring order, with France imposing partial curfews and Italy deploying soldiers, responses protesters say obscure their demands and could make things even worse. “Politicians are responding in ways that are completely disconnected from reality, completely absurd,” said Luis Marques, a 19-year-old psychology student in Lisbon. Students are demanding action on soaring rents, more spending on education instead of defence and more job opportunities for young people. But experts say the unrest reflects a broader sense among many young Europeans that they have been shut out of politics and sidelined. “These young people do not just feel like they do not have a place in politics, they feel they are not being heard at all,” said Geoffrey Pleyers, president of the International Sociological Association. Rosario Forlenza, a professor at Rome’s Luiss University, called it a “European generational revolt” rooted in a social and economic crisis “to which politicians cannot give a substantive response”. “Young people are a minority of the population that is shrinking and so their social, economic, cultural, political and electoral weight is becoming ever more irrelevant,” he said. ‘Inspiring other people’ The anger has been particularly palpable in France and Italy, where fresh demonstrations are planned for Saturday. “People are very angry, they’ve had enough. Working hard all day and still not being able to fill up their shopping cart,” a 20-year-old student who gave his name as Eddy told AFP at a protest in Bordeaux last weekend. “Will smashing everything change anything? I think it can be a jolt to wake up the politicians. We don’t know what else to do to make ourselves heard. The ballot box? We don’t believe in it anymore,” he said. Firefighters extinguish a fire in a bar during a demonstration in Paris against the high cost of living. Police estimated nearly 200,000 people took part in protests across France, while organisers claimed a turnout of almost 800,000.—AFP Protest movements across Europe are increasingly drawing inspiration from one another, and even looking to youth-led movements further afield in places like Bangladesh, India and Nepal. In Italy, one student slogan last week urged protesters to “do as in France”, while shared symbols, including the Jolly Roger pirate flag, have become common across youth rallies. Marcos Navarro, 22, a laboratory quality-control technician from Madrid, said protesters across Europe were meeting to share tactics. “They’ve come to ask us: ‘How did you do it? How do you organise yourselves?’ We’ve already exchanged ideas,” said Navarro, who has been camping with hundreds of others in Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol square since September to protest housing costs and evictions. Ayla Herrero, a 26-year-old anthropologist helping at the camp’s infirmary, said it was “inspiring for us to know that we’re inspiring other people, that it doesn’t just stay here”. ‘Not acceptable’ Concern about the rise in military spending in Europe following the Russian invasion of Ukraine has also been a rallying point. Nikos Mavroudis, a 17-year-old high school student in Athens’ Exarchia neighbourhood, said the money could be better spent on his school, where chunks of plaster are falling. “It’s not acceptable for classrooms to be dangerous,” said Mavroudis, who hopes to become a cook and plans to move elsewhere in Europe to “countries where things are better”. Protesting students gather and hold placards as they carry out a blockading action at the Turgot secondary school, in Paris, on October 5, 2026. — AFP At Rome’s occupied Morgagni high school, where students have barricaded entrances with desks, protesters pointed to the crumbling infrastructure as evidence of neglect. An 18-year-old, who did not want to be named, said the media and politicians in Italy were focusing too heavily on looting and vandalism by some protesters. “It turns hatred against the students who are victims of this system,” he said. Asked about the violence, Sabrina Brizzola, 24, coordinator of the Italian University Students’ Union, said organisations like hers should “organise and channel this generational rage”. “We have shared concerns, even if our ways of protesting differ,” she said.

articles.title: France to deploy 70,000 police for fresh weekend protests
articles.description: France will deploy about 70,000 police nationwide as it braces for new protests on Saturday after some of the worst urban violence in years erupted on the sidelines of demonstrations a week ago. Protests by high school students over learning conditions sparked a movement that has since spread nationwide, fuelled by broader anger over the rising cost of living. About 70,000 security personnel will be deployed on Saturday, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said at a news conference in Paris, warning that calls for violence and looting were circulating on social media. The protests have come at a critical moment for France six months ahead of elections to replace President Emmanuel Macron, with a new poll underlining far-right candidate Marine Le Pen as the frontrunner and indicating her position has been strengthened by the latest events. Adding to tensions, Le Pen is due at the weekend to host her National Rally (RN) party congress in Orleans, with thousands of supporters expected and local authorities fearing clashes as counter-protesters also head to the city south of Paris. Macron met representatives of secondary school pupils on Friday, but they emerged from the talks urging students to keep protesting until the government put forward concrete proposals to address their demands. Offenders jailed Macron’s government has sought to draw a line between the legitimate demands of protesters and the looting, burning and ransacking that erupted on the sidelines of demonstrations last Saturday. Courts have already sent 217 people, half of them first-time offenders, to prison over the events on Saturday, Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said. On Thursday, Macron called for “the utmost severity” against “acts of delinquency”, accusing “ultra-left” groups of having sought to “bring down the republic” last weekend. An extreme-left group in western France posted on its website a call for its supporters to be “uncatchable, unpredictable, to evade the deployment” of police. Protest restrictions Authorities have stepped up security measures and imposed restrictions on protests. In Orleans, between 20,000 and 30,000 people are expected to come out against Le Pen’s National Rally party, but the gathering will be barred from the city centre, the prefecture said. In the southeastern city of Lyon, central areas will also be off-limits to demonstrators this weekend. In Paris, police overturned a previous permit for union-led protesters to march between Bastille and Nation squares in the east. The force said the parade could instead go in the afternoon along an alternative route on the southeastern edge of the city. Unions vowed to push ahead on the banned route, citing safety concerns over the alternative. Authorities in Marseille had also banned protests but announced Friday that a union-organised demonstration would be allowed on an “exceptional basis” – the only one authorised in the southern Bouches-du-Rhone department. In the capital, leading museums including the Louvre will be closed on Saturday while the Art Basel art fair is being cut short. Police ‘responsibility’ The restrictions, including outright bans on protests in some cities, have drawn criticism. Amnesty International denounced what it called “a slide toward authoritarian practice”, saying the measures were “jeopardising the right to demonstrate peacefully”. About 20 percent more members of the security forces will be deployed this weekend following questions over police preparedness and intelligence gathering ahead of last week’s violence. “Police have a responsibility both to ensure that protests can take place peacefully and safely and to protect the public from violent disorder,” said Eva Cosse, senior Europe researcher at Human Rights Watch. She voiced alarm over reports of children being severely injured by crowd-control weapons during recent gatherings. The violence has tarnished the image of France ahead of elections that could be a turning point in its modern history, with the government’s debt pile also troubling investors. A new poll by Harris Interactive for M6/RTL made after the violence showed Le Pen soaring ahead on 33-35 percent in the first round of voting for the presidential elections. It predicted that hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon was on course to face her in the run-off where Le Pen would emerge as an easy winner on about 70 percent of the vote.

articles.title: Police fire tear gas as new French demonstrations kick off
articles.description: French police started firing tear gas at protesters Saturday as they stepped up security in major cities, aiming to prevent a repeat of rioting a week ago, on a day of fresh nationwide demonstrations over the high cost of living. Police in the southeast city of Lyon fired tear gas to disperse some 150 protesters near the city centre — where demonstrations had been banned — when they briefly tried to block a road, an AFP journalist saw. Elsewhere, authorities and rattled shopkeepers geared up for potential new street violence. Near Paris’s Bastille neighbourhood, a clothing store had removed all its merchandise from shelves ahead of the demonstrations, while a nearby restaurant was boarded up with signs insisting it was “still open”. Many other retailers in the capital also had wooden boards covering their windows. Police officers stand guard at the Place de la Bastille with The July Column in the background ahead of a demonstration in Paris, France on October 24, 2026. — AFP The Louvre and the Musee d’Orsay museums were closed. Police were seen readying riot gear in zones that bore the brunt of last weekend’s clashes and looting. They were among 70,000 security personnel the interior ministry said were mobilised to counter the “high” threat of violence. “We will not tolerate any unrest,” Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said on Friday, adding that calls had been circulating on social media calling for violence and looting. Protest against far-right party Adding to tensions, far-right leader Marine Le Pen’s National Rally (RN) party was holding a weekend congress in the central city of Orleans to kick off her campaign for elections in six months to choose President Emmanuel Macron’s successor. Thousands of people yelling anti-fascist slogans marched on Saturday against Le Pen, and also against Macron, a pro-business centrist leader. “Macron resign. Le Pen in prison,” the crowd yelled. Protesters march along the Avenue Jean Zay during a demonstration ‘against racism, fascism and imperialism’ on the sidelines of the Congress of the Far-right party Rassemblement National (RN) in Orleans, central France on October 24, 2026. — AFP The violence last weekend and the heightened tensions over this weekend’s demonstrations highlighted the febrile atmosphere in France ahead of that vote, which Le Pen is best-placed, according to surveys, to win. Last weekend saw rioters on the margins of the nationwide demonstrations clash with police , vandalise public buildings and loot hundreds of stores. Some 2,700 people were arrested and the retail sector said shopowners were left with damage and stolen stock totalling hundreds of millions of euros. Macron attributed the worst of the violence to “ultra-left” groups that he said “want to bring down the republic”. Groups organising Saturday’s renewed demonstrations have accused Macron and his government of ignoring widespread public anger over rising costs, and over classroom conditions for students. Inflation in France, as elsewhere, has been sent surging by the Middle East war , started in February by US President Donald Trump and Israel. Protests have also been taking place in Italy, Belgium, Spain and Portugal over different issues, yet with some overlap on inflation and education problems. Italy has sent 500 troops to try to quell street violence in Milan. Boarded-up shops In Paris, streets on Saturday were unusually quiet, with many shop windows boarded up, and some of the bigger retailers sent messages to customers warning that they were closed for the day. The capital’s police at the last minute ordered a union-organised march in the city to be moved from Bastille, in the centre-east, to the more remote eastern Porte d’Italie on the southern rim of the capital. A woman walks past the boarded-up ground-floor windows of a historic building ahead of a demonstration planned for October 24, in central Bordeaux, southwestern France on October 23, 2026. — AFP Unions said they reluctantly would go along with that. But the Yellow Vest movement — a loosely organised grouping that staged disruptive street protests against Macron eight years ago — indicated it would not comply. Macron and his government have sought to draw a line between the legitimate demands of protesters and the looting, burning and ransacking that erupted on the sidelines of demonstrations last Saturday. Courts have already sent 217 people, half of them first-time offenders, to prison over the events on Saturday, officials said. Macron has said authorities would accept only union-led demonstrations and would counter any others they deemed “illegitimate”. Authorities in Marseille had banned all protests but announced Friday that a union-organised demonstration would be allowed on an “exceptional basis”. The restrictions, including outright bans on protests in some cities, have drawn criticism. Amnesty International denounced what it called “a slide toward authoritarian practice”, saying the measures were “jeopardising the right to demonstrate peacefully”. “Police have a responsibility both to ensure that protests can take place peacefully and safely and to protect the public from violent disorder,” said Eva Cosse, senior Europe researcher at Human Rights Watch.

articles.title: Protestos na França ocorrem sob forte esquema de segurança
articles.description: Manifestantes se reuniram em Paris e em cidades de toda a França neste sábado (24), sob a vigilância de 70 mil policiais, enquanto o governo tentava evitar a repetição dos distúrbios e saques que sacudiram o país no fim de semana passado. O ministro do Interior, Laurent Nuñez, disse que 135 pessoas haviam sido presas em todo o país até o início da tarde, muitas após revistas preventivas que encontraram fogos de artifício, rolamentos de esferas e outros objetos que poderiam ser usados como armas. Notícias relacionadas: França quer impor toques de recolher após fim de semana com tumultos. Alunos e professores protestam na França no maior dia de mobilização. Tensões voltam a crescer; França contabiliza custos de protestos. “Temos que ser extremamente ágeis. Recebemos muitos avisos sobre desordem, tanto de grupos políticos quanto, simplesmente, de criminosos”, disse aos jornalistas. “Vai ser um dia longo.” Enquanto o início da principal marcha em Paris transcorria de forma pacífica, a polícia usou gás lacrimogêneo contra multidões em Lyon, a terceira maior cidade da França. O governo mobilizou 10 mil policiais a mais do que em 17 de outubro, dia em que protestos contra o custo de vida e a deterioração dos serviços públicos se transformaram em alguns dos piores distúrbios que a França viu em anos. Lojas e museus fechados Grande parte do centro de Paris parecia uma cidade em lockdown, com lojistas fechando as vitrines com tapumes, museus com as portas fechadas e mais de 20 estações de metrô interditadas. Entidades empresariais pediram que os varejistas permanecessem fechados depois que milhares de lojas e negócios foram danificados ou saqueados em toda a França no último fim de semana. “Quase não há clientes, então não vale a pena ficar aberto”, disse Oskar, gerente de uma boutique Kiton em Paris. Vários dos mais conhecidos centros culturais da capital, incluindo o Louvre, o Musée d’Orsay e a Ópera de Paris, fecharam como precaução, deixando os turistas frustrados. “Está tudo fechado com tapumes e não sabemos bem para onde ir”, disse Xavier Dolliole, turista da cidade norte-americana de Nova Orleans. A rota da principal manifestação em Paris só foi definida após uma batalha judicial, desencadeada por uma ordem policial de última hora, que afastava os organizadores do centro da cidade em direção às regiões do sudeste da capital. A polícia argumentou que o trajeto original passava por áreas com alta concentração de empresas semelhantes às atacadas no fim de semana anterior. Líderes de esquerda disseram que a mudança tardia tinha como objetivo causar confusão e afastar as pessoas. “Mais uma vez, os que estão no poder criam transtornos para as marchas e prazos impossíveis para que as organizações se reorganizem”, disse o líder da esquerda radical Jean-Luc Mélenchon, que se juntou aos manifestantes nas ruas de Paris. Congresso Muitos manifestantes acusaram o governo de reagir de forma exagerada, com soldados enviados para patrulhar a Champs-Élysées. “Choramos pelas lojas, não pelas pessoas que são empobrecidas o ano todo”, disse Clara Lebbadi, estudante de artes de 22 anos. “Minha amiga e eu quase não viemos porque estávamos com medo, mas viemos justamente porque é importante não deixar a repressão vencer”, acrescentou. A primeira marcha autorizada neste sábado transcorreu pacificamente em Orléans, a cerca de 120 quilômetros ao sul de Paris, onde manifestantes protestaram contra o Reagrupamento Nacional, de Marine Le Pen, que realizava um congresso partidário na cidade. As tensões aumentaram após tiros na sexta-feira (23), a oeste de Paris, quando um atirador, suspeito de agir por ódio islamofóbico, matou uma pessoa e feriu mais quatro, entre elas uma menina de 12 anos. “Viemos dizer à extrema direita, cara a cara, que não temos medo”, disse Bally Bagayoko, prefeito de Saint-Denis e membro do partido de esquerda radical França Insubmissa (LFI). *( Reportagem adicional de Crispian Balmer, Bertrand Boucey, Alessandro Parodi e Elizabeth Pineau ) *É proibida a reprodução deste conteúdo.

articles.title: Indian protesters clash with police over dam project bordering China
articles.description: Indian protesters angry over a proposed Himalayan mega-dam, intended to counter an upstream Chinese hydropower project, have clashed with police and torched buildings, officials said. The violence in Arunachal Pradesh state erupted late on Friday during protests against the proposed 11,200-megawatt Siang Upper Multipurpose Project of state-run hydropower company NHPC, Chief Minister Pema Khandu told reporters on Saturday. “The mob destroyed a lot of properties, police station, the NHPC office was vandalised, several elected representatives’ homes were ransacked,” Khandu told reporters. Around 40 police personnel were injured by stones thrown by protesters, who also vandalised the NHPC’s offices. Police fired tear gas canisters to disperse the crowd. Khandu urged opponents of the project to engage with the government. “Question us, have dialogue with us, instead of violence,” Khandu said. India says the proposed dam is needed to counter China’s $167-billion Yaxia project, a likely record-breaking hydropower scheme upstream in Tibet. New Delhi fears the Chinese project could affect water flows downstream, and says the proposed Indian dam would create a vast reservoir to store water and help maintain flows into the Brahmaputra river. Beijing has said its project will have no “negative impact” downstream. China says Arunachal Pradesh, which Beijing calls Zangnan, is a part of South Tibet — a claim India has repeatedly dismissed. India’s proposed dam, which would be by far its largest hydropower project, has drawn fierce opposition from local communities who fear the loss of their homes and land. The project underscores tensions between the two most populous countries, which share a disputed Himalayan border patrolled by tens of thousands of troops. India’s foreign ministry said on Friday the two sides remained in regular contact to manage border tensions, after a top Indian border police official Shatrujeet Kapur reported “face offs” between Indian and Chinese forces.
